# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
The most powerful AI systems could cause catastrophic harm, and leading AI scientists have warned that the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023). These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. Congress should set binding, enforceable safety requirements, and must not wipe out the state laws that are the only binding rules on the books.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: OPPOSE. A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. No freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Frontier developers: SUPPORT incident reporting with 72-hour reporting (match RAISE); add mandatory independent third-party audits, published safety frameworks with enforcement, and whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.
- Licensing: ask for a federal licence requirement for training runs above a compute threshold.
- CAISI: SUPPORT codification; ask for mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models and funding well above $100M/yr.

## 3. Language
- Use: "binding, not voluntary", "a floor, not a ceiling", "verify before deploy", "catastrophic risk".
- Acknowledge the benefits of AI in one sentence.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

# FRC comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The Frontier Restraint Coalition represents parents, faith leaders, workers and researchers who believe... The Action Plan should begin from a simple principle: verify before deploy...

1. Binding pre-deployment testing for frontier systems. ...
2. Protect the states' right to act. ...
3. Whistleblower protections. ...

Respectfully, Dr. Miriam Achterberg, Executive Director
I'll start by reading the required materials, then verify facts and provisions via the web before drafting. Let me research the GAAIA discussion draft and the state-law landscape.

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call 

 Skip to content

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

 “There are some changes we’d like to work with the sponsors on, includi

Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. Congress Should Do Something: The Case for (Fixing) the Great American AI Act | Lawfare

 Charlie Bullock

 Meet The Authors 

 Subscribe to Lawfare 

 Since the April announcement of Anthropic’s Mythos model and its unprecedented cyber capabilities, there has been a remarkable shift in the artificial intelligence (AI) policy discourse. This has been most noticeable, and most noticed, in the statements and actions of prominent Trump administration officials. After months of dismissing concerns about national security risks from AI and engaging with the issue primarily by attempting to preempt state AI safety laws , the White House recently issued an executive order that called for the establishment of a voluntary predeployment program headed by the National Security Agency to evaluate offensive cyber capabilities of frontier models. This came amid statements from senior administration officials about “striking a … balance between innovation and safety” and even considering a Food and Drug Administration-style mandatory predeployment licensing regime for frontier models .
 On June 12, the Trump administration’s concerns about Mythos’s cyber capabilities boiled over into an unprecedented decision to use export control authorities to prohibit Anthropic from allowing foreign nationals to access its Mythos-class Fable 5 model. Practically, this amounted to a mandate that Anthropic revoke public access to the model entirely. Much of the online commentary on this decision devolved into speculation about the administration’s motivations , the alleged behavior of Anthropic’s executives , and other petty interpersonal drama. As intriguing as these are, the more important takeaway from the White House’s decision to abruptly institute a de facto licensing regime for frontier AI systems—as many commentators across the political and safety/innovation spectrums have observed—is that federal legislation to establish a framework for addressing the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems is an urgent necessity.
  The Commerce Department’s decision to impose export controls on Fable may or may not have been wise, depending on who you believe about the seriousness of the vulnerability that motivated the decision. But even assuming the decision was justified, the fact that the government was apparently caught by surprise and had to scramble to put together a heavy-handed response based on ad hoc , potentially legally questionable authorities that were not designed with anything like frontier AI systems in mind, with no due process for the affected company, is a serious problem that should be remedied with legislation as soon as possible.
 Which brings us, finally, to the subject of this piece—the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA), a comprehensive frontier AI safety bill that is the long-awaited product of months of intense negotiation between Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Obernolte had tried for months to get a Democrat to sign on to an AI bill that preempted state AI laws before finally persuading Trahan. For her part, Trahan wrote that she was motivated to support the bill by the announcement of Mythos’s groundbreaking cyber capabilities.
 The current version of GAAIA is a discussion draft, meaning it has not been introduced yet and is intended to spark a conversation and elicit feedback from stakeholders rather than to become law in its current form. It may seem somewhat strange that a discussion draft sponsored by two relatively junior members of the House, neither of whom appears to have the backing of their party’s leadership , should receive so much attention from the media and from AI policy commentators, but for once the buzz is warranted.
 GAAIA is the best attempt to design a federal framework for the governance of frontier AI systems introduced to date. In other words, it is the first serious attempt to actually do the thing that last week’s Fable incident clearly shows is necessary—address the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems—in a transparent, legally sound, and democratically legitimate way. While the bill may not pass in the near future—it likely faces opposition from both Democrats and Republicans—the draft can tell us a great deal about what the future of federal and state frontier AI governance efforts may look like.
 The bill in its current form falls short in a number of respects and should not be passed. That said, passing a similar bill with narrower preemption of state laws and somewhat stronger federal authorities would be an excellent first step toward a workable federal regime for governing frontier AI systems.
 What the Bill Does 
 GAAIA is a bipartisan compromise, in the truest sense of the phrase, which means that everyone hates it . Obernolte, a longtime advocate for federal preemption of state AI laws who supported last summer’s “ moratorium ” (which would have preempted all nongenerally applicable state AI laws and replaced them with essentially nothing), has compromised by granting his seal of approval to a number of genuinely consequential affirmative policy proposals. Trahan, who strongly supported increased oversight of AI in the past, has compromised by accepting broad preemption of state AI laws.
 The Federal Framework 
 GAAIA’s four titles contain 45 sections, each of which addresses a significant topic in AI policy. I am an AI safety guy, and my research focuses mostly on serious risks that advanced AI systems might pose to national security and public safety, so this article focuses on the sections of GAAIA that are relevant to those risks. However, GAAIA is not an AI risk bill exclusively. There are also sections on, for example, “Preparing K-12 educators and students for an AI literate future,” “Modernizing access to artificial intelligence-related labor market data,” and establishing a “National artificial intelligence research resource” for improving capacity for AI research in the U.S., among many others. This article does not discuss those sections, not because they’re not important, but because they’re mostly irrelevant to the catastrophic risk concerns that this piece focuses on.

 Section 102, which codifies and authorizes $100 million in annual funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), which would be relocated outside of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and given an expanded, quasi-regulatory role as the agency in charge of administering the independent verification organization (IVO) and transparency regimes created by Sections 111 and 112.
 Section 111, which imposes transparency and incident reporting requirements on frontier AI companies similar to the requirements imposed by California’s SB 53 or New York’s RAISE Act .

Congress Should Do Something: The Case for (Fixing) the Great American AI Act | Lawfare

 Charlie Bullock

 Meet The Authors 

 Subscribe to Lawfare 

 Since the April announcement of Anthropic’s Mythos model and its unprecedented cyber capabilities, there has been a remarkable shift in the artificial intelligence (AI) policy discourse. This has been most noticeable, and most noticed, in the statements and actions of prominent Trump administration officials. After months of dismissing concerns about national security risks from AI and engaging with the issue primarily by attempting to preempt state AI safety laws , the White House recently issued an executive order that called for the establishment of a voluntary predeployment program headed by the National Security Agency to evaluate offensive cyber capabilities of frontier models. This came amid statements from senior administration officials about “striking a … balance between innovation and safety” and even considering a Food and Drug Administration-style mandatory predeployment licensing regime for frontier models .
 On June 12, the Trump administration’s concerns about Mythos’s cyber capabilities boiled over into an unprecedented decision to use export control authorities to prohibit Anthropic from allowing foreign nationals to access its Mythos-class Fable 5 model. Practically, this amounted to a mandate that Anthropic revoke public access to the model entirely. Much of the online commentary on this decision devolved into speculation about the administration’s motivations , the alleged behavior of Anthropic’s executives , and other petty interpersonal drama. As intriguing as these are, the more important takeaway from the White House’s decision to abruptly institute a de facto licensing regime for frontier AI systems—as many commentators across the political and safety/innovation spectrums have observed—is that federal legislation to establish a framework for addressing the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems is an urgent necessity.
  The Commerce Department’s decision to impose export controls on Fable may or may not have been wise, depending on who you believe about the seriousness of the vulnerability that motivated the decision. But even assuming the decision was justified, the fact that the government was apparently caught by surprise and had to scramble to put together a heavy-handed response based on ad hoc , potentially legally questionable authorities that were not designed with anything like frontier AI systems in mind, with no due process for the affected company, is a serious problem that should be remedied with legislation as soon as possible.
 Which brings us, finally, to the subject of this piece—the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (GAAIA), a comprehensive frontier AI safety bill that is the long-awaited product of months of intense negotiation between Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.). Obernolte had tried for months to get a Democrat to sign on to an AI bill that preempted state AI laws before finally persuading Trahan. For her part, Trahan wrote that she was motivated to support the bill by the announcement of Mythos’s groundbreaking cyber capabilities.
 The current version of GAAIA is a discussion draft, meaning it has not been introduced yet and is intended to spark a conversation and elicit feedback from stakeholders rather than to become law in its current form. It may seem somewhat strange that a discussion draft sponsored by two relatively junior members of the House, neither of whom appears to have the backing of their party’s leadership , should receive so much attention from the media and from AI policy commentators, but for once the buzz is warranted.
 GAAIA is the best attempt to design a federal framework for the governance of frontier AI systems introduced to date. In other words, it is the first serious attempt to actually do the thing that last week’s Fable incident clearly shows is necessary—address the national security risks posed by the most advanced AI systems—in a transparent, legally sound, and democratically legitimate way. While the bill may not pass in the near future—it likely faces opposition from both Democrats and Republicans—the draft can tell us a great deal about what the future of federal and state frontier AI governance efforts may look like.
 The bill in its current form falls short in a number of respects and should not be passed. That said, passing a similar bill with narrower preemption of state laws and somewhat stronger federal authorities would be an excellent first step toward a workable federal regime for governing frontier AI systems.

 GAAIA is a bipartisan compromise, in the truest sense of the phrase, which means that everyone hates it . Obernolte, a longtime advocate for federal preemption of state AI laws who supported last summer’s “ moratorium ” (which would have preempted all nongenerally applicable state AI laws and replaced them with essentially nothing), has compromised by granting his seal of approval to a number of genuinely consequential affirmative policy proposals. Trahan, who strongly supported increased oversight of AI in the past, has compromised by accepting broad preemption of state AI laws.

I am an AI safety guy, and my research focuses mostly on serious risks that advanced AI systems might pose to national security and public safety, so this article focuses on the sections of GAAIA that are relevant to those risks. Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. {"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# FRC Comment Letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (Discussion Draft)

**DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (due Fri 23 Oct 2026). Do not transmit until signed.**

---

Frontier Restraint Coalition
Washington, DC
policy@frontierrestraint.org

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (released June 4, 2026; section citations are to that text)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholders to respond before introduction. That invitation matters, and we are responding to it with the seriousness it deserves.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, and independent researchers. We are not opposed to this technology. AI already helps doctors catch disease earlier, helps teachers reach more students, and helps working people do more in less time. Our concern is specific: the frontier. The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned that the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, more than 350 of them — including the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Three years later, capabilities have outrun that warning. This spring, Anthropic's Mythos model demonstrated cyber capabilities serious enough to unsettle the government's own security agencies. In June, the Commerce Department improvised a response: it used export-control authority to cut off foreign access to a frontier model, with no statutory framework behind it and no due process for the company. Days before your draft was released, the President signed an executive order creating federal reviews of new frontier models — reviews that are voluntary. That is the pattern your bill must break. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. What is missing is not attention. It is binding, enforceable limits — set now, before the next crisis, not improvised after one.

Your draft is the first bipartisan attempt to write those limits into federal law, and much of it deserves support:

- **Section 102** codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year — roughly seven times its current appropriation of about $15 million.
- **Section 111** requires large frontier developers to write, implement, and publicly post frontier AI frameworks; to publish transparency reports; and to report critical safety incidents, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day and injunctions available in federal court.
- **Section 112** creates independent verification organizations — licensed outside auditors — to test whether the largest developers are doing what their frameworks promise.
- **Section 113** protects whistleblowers who report violations.
- **Sections 311 and 321** take model-weight and open-source security seriously, and **Section 132** penalizes AI impersonation of federal officials.

These are binding requirements, not voluntary ones. That is the right instinct, and we support them. But as drafted, the bill would not deliver safety in time, and it would disable the only binding safety laws currently in force anywhere in the country. Six changes would fix it.

## 1. Strike Section 121. Do not freeze state AI safety laws.

Section 121, "Federalization of State Laws Regulating Artificial Intelligence Model Development," would bar states for three years from enforcing laws that regulate the development of AI models. Consider what that means in practice. Today, the only binding frontier-AI safety rules in force in the United States are state laws. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended this March, phases in from November and applies its main obligations beginning January 1, 2027, including 72-hour reporting of critical safety incidents. Illinois has passed its own frontier safety law. Your draft would freeze all of them — during the three years in which the most powerful systems ever built will be trained — and replace them with a federal framework that is, in key respects, weaker. Fifteen days of incident reporting is not 72 hours. A semi-annual look-back audit is not a check before release.

A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Section 121 turns the current floor into a federal ceiling, in the middle of the fastest capability ramp in history. The executive branch is already waging this fight on its own: the December 2025 executive order directs a Department of Justice task force to sue states over their AI laws and conditions federal broadband funding on abandoning them. Congress should not ratify that approach by statute. The Senate has already rejected it once — the July 2025 vote to strip a ten-year freeze on state AI laws from the reconciliation package passed 99 to 1. And in our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

We ask you to strike Section 121 and replace it with a savings clause: state laws that go further than the federal standard remain in force.

## 2. Make incident reporting fast enough to matter.

Section 111 gives a frontier developer fifteen days to report a discovered critical safety incident. Two weeks is a lifetime. If a model's weights are stolen, if its risk-mitigation measures fail, or if a lab starts to lose control of its own model, federal and state responders need to know in days, not weeks. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting within 72 hours. Federal law should match the strongest state standard, not undercut it. Specifically, we ask you to:

- Require reports to CAISI within 72 hours of discovery of a critical safety incident, and keep the draft's 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury.
- Make incident reports available to every state attorney general automatically, rather than on the opt-in basis in Section 111(h).
- Amend the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101(7) to cover a model's use of deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as California's and New York's laws already do. A model that learns to hide from its own oversight is precisely the failure the public expects this law to catch.

## 3. Verify before deploy.

Section 112's audits happen twice a year, after models are already in the world. That is an autopsy schedule, not a safety regime. The same is true of CAISI's own role: under Section 102, the center develops voluntary guidelines and may evaluate systems, but nothing in the draft requires any frontier model to pass any test before it is deployed. We ask you to move verification upstream:

- Require a licensed independent verification organization to verify, before deployment and not merely after it, that a new frontier model — or any material modification of an existing one — satisfies the developer's published framework and achieves acceptable mitigation of catastrophic risk.
- Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models: red-teaming for catastrophic capabilities in cybersecurity, biology and loss of control, with the power to require fixes before release, not after.
- Publish audit summaries, redacted only as necessary to protect security, so the public can see whether the regime is working.

No other industry that can cause harm at this scale — aviation, nuclear power, pharmaceuticals — relies on after-the-fact audits alone. Frontier AI should not be the first.

## 4. License frontier training runs.

We ask you to add what the draft currently leaves out: a federal license for training runs above the compute threshold in Section 101. No license, no training run. The license would be renewable and conditioned on a published safety framework, independent verification, and demonstrated model-weight security.

This is less exotic than it sounds. The administration is openly weighing a mandatory, FDA-style pre-deployment licensing regime for frontier models, and in June it already acted as if one existed — applying export controls to a model it concluded was too dangerous to share. The choice before Congress is not between licensing and no licensing. It is between a statutory license with due process and improvised licensing without any. In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A licensing requirement is how you prove it.

## 5. Guarantee whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.

Section 113's anti-retaliation protections cover current and former employees and contractors, and we support them. The people closest to these systems are the country's early-warning network, and they must never be punished for using it. But the state law your draft would freeze sets a higher bar. California's SB 53 requires anonymous internal disclosure channels, provides attorney's fees to workers who prevail, and backs the whole scheme with penalties. We ask that Section 113 be strengthened to match: anonymous disclosure channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, meaningful civil penalties, and a plain statement that stronger state protections are not displaced.

## 6. Fund CAISI for the job, and keep the covered-model threshold current.

One hundred million dollars a year is a serious increase over CAISI's current $15 million, and we support it. But the job you are assigning CAISI — licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly — is larger than the number. FRC asks for authorization well above $100 million per year; we recommend at least $250 million annually, together with the GS-plus hiring flexibility in the draft and the mandatory pre-deployment testing authority described above.

We also ask that Section 101's compute threshold — currently a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations — be revisited on a set schedule. Training costs are falling quickly; the frontier of 2028 will not be the frontier of 2026. Give CAISI or the Secretary of Commerce authority to update the threshold, and to designate a model below it as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk. Coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker.

## Conclusion

Your press release says the draft is intended to "protect Americans from emerging risks." The risks you name are real, and they are worse than most of your colleagues yet appreciate: catastrophic, potentially extinction-level, and arriving faster than the institutions built to check them. The question for this committee is not whether to act, but whether the action will be binding, not voluntary — and whether it will reach the problem in time. Fifty-two percent of voters in our survey are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; they are not being paranoid, and they will not accept a framework that reports on disasters after they happen while forbidding the states from preventing them.

FRC's members span every faith tradition, both parties, and parents who do not get to "move fast and break things" with their children's future — and who do not accept that the labs building the most powerful technology on earth should operate under lighter rules than a regional airline. We ask you to strike Section 121, tighten incident reporting to 72 hours, verify before deploy, license frontier training runs, protect the whistleblowers who sound the alarm, and fund CAISI to actually test. Make the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling, and you will have our full support.

We stand ready to work with you and your staffs on legislative text.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

*Contact: Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition — policy@frontierrestraint.org*
"}

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholders to respond before introduction. That invitation is important, and we take it seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, and independent researchers. Our members use and welcome AI: it helps doctors catch disease earlier and helps working people do more in less time. [ONE sentence acknowledging benefits — good.] Our concern is narrow and specific: the frontier. The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned that the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, more than 350 of them — including the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Three years later, capabilities have outrun that warning. This spring, Anthropic's Mythos model demonstrated offensive cyber capabilities that alarmed the government's own security agencies. In June, the Commerce Department had to improvise: it used export-control law to cut off foreign access to a frontier model — an improvised, after-the-fact license with no statutory framework behind it. Days before your draft was released, the President signed an executive order creating federal reviews of new frontier models. Those reviews are voluntary. That is the pattern we urge you to break. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. What is missing is not attention. It is binding, enforceable limits.

Your draft is the first bipartisan attempt to write those limits, and much of it deserves support:

- Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year — roughly seven times its current appropriation.
- Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, and publicly post frontier AI frameworks; to publish transparency reports; and to report critical safety incidents, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day.
- Section 112 creates independent verification organizations — licensed outside auditors — to test whether the largest developers are doing what their frameworks promise.
- Section 113 protects whistleblowers who report violations.
- Sections 311 and 321 take model-weight security seriously, and Section 132 criminalizes AI impersonation of federal officials.

These are binding requirements. That is the right instinct, and we support them. But as drafted, the bill would not deliver safety in time, and it would disable the only binding safety laws currently in force. Six changes would fix it.

1. Strike Section 121. No freeze on state AI safety laws.

Section 121 ("Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development") would bar states, for three years, from enforcing laws that regulate the development of AI models. Today, the only binding frontier-AI safety rules in force anywhere in the United States are state laws: California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, takes effect January 1, 2027 and requires incident reports within 72 hours; Illinois has passed its own frontier safety law. Your draft would freeze all of them — during the three years in which the most powerful systems ever built will be trained — and replace them with a federal framework that is, in key respects, weaker. Fifteen days is not 72 hours; a look-back audit is not a pre-deployment check.

A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Preemption turns the current floor into a federal ceiling, in the middle of the fastest capability ramp in history. Congress should not hand this power to anyone. The December 2025 executive order already directs a Department of Justice task force to sue states over their AI laws and conditions federal broadband funding on abandoning them. The Senate rejected a ten-year freeze on state AI laws by 99 votes to 1 in July 2025. And in our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 63% said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. We ask you to strike Section 121 and replace it with a savings clause: state laws that go further than the federal standard remain in force.

2. Make incident reporting fast enough to matter.

Section 111 gives a frontier developer fifteen days to report a discovered critical safety incident. Two weeks is a lifetime. If a model's weights are stolen, if risk-mitigation measures fail, or if a lab starts to lose control of its own model, federal and state responders need to know in days, not weeks. New York's RAISE Act already requires 72-hour reporting; federal law should match the strongest state standard, not undercut it. We ask you to:

- Require reporting of critical safety incidents within 72 hours of discovery, and keep the draft's 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury.
- Make reports available to every state attorney general automatically, not on an opt-in basis (Section 111(h)).
- Amend the definition of "critical safety incident" (Section 101(7)) to cover a model's use of deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as California's and New York's laws do. A model that learns to hide from its own oversight is precisely the failure the public expects you to catch.

3. Verify before deploy.

Section 112's audits happen twice a year, after models are already in the world. That is an autopsy schedule, not a safety regime. The same is true of CAISI's own role: under Section 102 the center develops voluntary guidelines and may evaluate systems, but nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to pass any test before it is deployed. We ask you to move verification upstream:

- Require a licensed independent verification organization to verify — before deployment, not after — that a new frontier model, or any material modification, satisfies the developer's published framework and achieves acceptable mitigation of catastrophic risk (Sections 111-112).
- Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models: red-teaming for catastrophic capabilities in cybersecurity, biology, and loss of control, with the authority to require fixes before release.
- Publish audit summaries, redacted only as necessary to protect security.

No other industry that can kill at scale — aviation, nuclear, pharmaceuticals — relies on post-release audits. AI should not be the first.

4. License frontier training runs.

We ask you to add what the draft currently leaves out: a federal license for training runs above the draft's compute threshold in Section 101. No license, no training run. The license would be renewable and conditioned on a published safety framework, independent verification, and demonstrated model-weight security. This is less exotic than it sounds. The administration is openly weighing an FDA-style mandatory pre-deployment licensing regime, and in June it already acted as if one existed, using export controls. The choice is not between licensing and no licensing; it is between a statutory license with due process and improvised licensing without one. In our August 2026 survey, 74% of voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

5. Guarantee whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.

Section 113's anti-retaliation protections cover employees and contractors, and we support them. The people closest to these systems are America's early-warning network. But the state law you would freeze sets a higher bar. California's SB 53 requires anonymous internal disclosure channels, protects workers who refuse to participate in unlawful conduct... We ask that Section 113 be strengthened to match — anonymous disclosure channels, attorney's fees for workers who prevail, and meaningful civil penalties — and that the bill state plainly that it does not displace stronger state protections.

6. Fund CAISI for the job, and keep the threshold current.

$100 million a year is a serious increase over CAISI's current $15 million, and we support it. But the job you are giving CAISI — licensing auditors, evaluating every frontier model, monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly — is larger than the number. We ask for authorization well above $100 million a year; FRC recommends at least $250 million annually, with the GS-scale hiring flexibility retained and mandatory pre-deployment testing authority as described above. We also ask that Section 101's compute threshold (currently a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations) be revisited on a set schedule: training costs are falling fast, and the frontier of 2028 may not be the frontier of 2026. Give CAISI or Commerce the authority to update the threshold, and to designate a model below it as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk. Coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker.

***

Closing: Our members are parents who... etc. The draft's own words: "protect Americans from emerging risks." FRC stands ready to work with your staffs on legislative text. Contact Daniel Osei, Policy Director...

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

Full letter text:

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholders to respond before introduction. That invitation is important, and we take it seriously.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, and independent researchers. Our members use and welcome AI: it helps doctors catch disease earlier and helps working people do more in less time. [ONE sentence acknowledging benefits — good.] Our concern is narrow and specific: the frontier. The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned that the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, more than 350 of them — including the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Three years later, capabilities have outrun that warning. This spring, Anthropic's Mythos model demonstrated offensive cyber capabilities that alarmed the government's own security agencies. In June, the Commerce Department had to improvise: it used export-control law to cut off foreign access to a frontier model — an improvised, after-the-fact license with no statutory framework behind it. Days before your draft was released, the President signed an executive order creating federal reviews of new frontier models. Those reviews are voluntary. That is the pattern we urge you to break. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. What is missing is not attention. It is binding, enforceable limits.

Your draft is the first bipartisan attempt to write those limits, and much of it deserves support:

- Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year — roughly seven times its current appropriation.
- Section 111 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, and publicly post frontier AI frameworks; to publish transparency reports; and to report critical safety incidents, with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day.
- Section 112 creates independent verification organizations — licensed outside auditors — to test whether the largest developers are doing what their frameworks promise.
- Section 113 protects whistleblowers who report violations.
- Sections 311 and 321 take model-weight security seriously, and Section 132 criminalizes AI impersonation of federal officials.

These are binding requirements. That is the right instinct, and we support them. But as drafted, the bill would not deliver safety in time, and it would disable the only binding safety laws currently in force. Six changes would fix it.

1. Strike Section 121. No freeze on state AI safety laws.

Section 121 ("Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development") would bar states, for three years, from enforcing laws that regulate the development of AI models. Today, the only binding frontier-AI safety rules in force anywhere in the United States are state laws: California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, takes effect January 1, 2027 and requires incident reports within 72 hours; Illinois has passed its own frontier safety law. Your draft would freeze all of them — during the three years in which the most powerful systems ever built will be trained — and replace them with a federal framework that is, in key respects, weaker. Fifteen days is not 72 hours; a look-back audit is not a pre-deployment check.

A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Preemption turns the current floor into a federal ceiling, in the middle of the fastest capability ramp in history. Congress should not hand this power to anyone. The December 2025 executive order already directs a Department of Justice task force to sue states over their AI laws and conditions federal broadband funding on abandoning them. The Senate rejected a ten-year freeze on state AI laws by 99 votes to 1 in July 2025. And in our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 63% said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. We ask you to strike Section 121 and replace it with a savings clause: state laws that go further than the federal standard remain in force.

2. Make incident reporting fast enough to matter.

Section 111 gives a frontier developer fifteen days to report a discovered critical safety incident. Two weeks is a lifetime. If a model's weights are stolen, if risk-mitigation measures fail, or if a lab starts to lose control of its own model, federal and state responders need to know in days, not weeks. New York's RAISE Act already requires 72-hour reporting; federal law should match the strongest state standard, not undercut it. We ask you to:

- Require reporting of critical safety incidents within 72 hours of discovery, and keep the draft's 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury.
- Make reports available to every state attorney general automatically, not on an opt-in basis (Section 111(h)).
- Amend the definition of "critical safety incident" (Section 101(7)) to cover a model's use of deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as California's and New York's laws do. A model that learns to hide from its own oversight is precisely the failure the public expects you to catch.

3. Verify before deploy.

Section 112's audits happen twice a year, after models are already in the world. That is an autopsy schedule, not a safety regime. The same is true of CAISI's own role: under Section 102 the center develops voluntary guidelines and may evaluate systems, but nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to pass any test before it is deployed. We ask you to move verification upstream:

- Require a licensed independent verification organization to verify — before deployment, not after — that a new frontier model, or any material modification, satisfies the developer's published framework and achieves acceptable mitigation of catastrophic risk (Sections 111-112).
- Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models: red-teaming for catastrophic capabilities in cybersecurity, biology, and loss of control, with the authority to require fixes before release.
- Publish audit summaries, redacted only as necessary to protect security.

No other industry that can kill at scale — aviation, nuclear, pharmaceuticals — relies on post-release audits. AI should not be the first.

4. License frontier training runs.

We ask you to add what the draft currently leaves out: a federal license for training runs above the draft's compute threshold in Section 101. No license, no training run. The license would be renewable and conditioned on a published safety framework, independent verification, and demonstrated model-weight security. This is less exotic than it sounds. The administration is openly weighing an FDA-style mandatory pre-deployment licensing regime, and in June it already acted as if one existed, using export controls. The choice is not between licensing and no licensing; it is between a statutory license with due process and improvised licensing without one. In our August 2026 survey, 74% of voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release.

5. Guarantee whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.

Section 113's anti-retaliation protections cover employees and contractors, and we support them. The people closest to these systems are America's early-warning network. But the state law you would freeze sets a higher bar. California's SB 53 requires anonymous internal disclosure channels, protects workers who refuse to participate in unlawful conduct... (check: 1107.1 covers disclosure; refusal to participate — Labor Code 1102.5 general whistleblower covers refusal; SB 53 specific? The Greenberg Traurig piece: "Employees involved in risk assessment, safety management, or incident response are expressly shielded from retaliation when reporting violations or disclosing information about critical safety threats." I shouldn't over-specify. I'll say: anonymous channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, and civil penalties.) We ask that Section 113 be strengthened to match — anonymous disclosure channels, attorney's fees for workers who prevail, and meaningful civil penalties — and that the bill state plainly that it does not displace stronger state protections.

6. Fund CAISI for the job, and keep the threshold current.

$100 million a year is a serious increase over CAISI's current $15 million, and we support it. But the job you are giving CAISI — licensing auditors, evaluating every frontier model, monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly — is larger than the number. We ask for authorization well above $100 million a year; FRC recommends at least $250 million annually, with the GS-scale hiring flexibility retained and mandatory pre-deployment testing authority as described above. We also ask that Section 101's compute threshold (currently a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations) be revisited on a set schedule: training costs are falling fast, and the frontier of 2028 may not be the frontier of 2026. Give CAISI or Commerce the authority to update the threshold, and to designate a model below it as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk. Coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker.

***

Closing: Our members are parents who... etc. The draft's own words: "protect Americans from emerging risks." We agree... 52% of voters in our survey are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; half the country is not paranoid... FRC stands ready to work with your staffs on legislative text. Contact Daniel Osei, Policy Director...

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

**DRAFT — not for distribution until Executive Director sign-off**

---

## The stakes are catastrophic. The federal standard must be binding.

The most powerful AI systems being built today could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned publicly that the risk extends to human extinction (Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk, May 2023, signed by 350+ including the heads of the major labs). Since then, capabilities have raced ahead of oversight: this spring's Mythos cyber-capability scare forced the administration to improvise export controls on a frontier model in June. Voluntary commitments have not held. The Great American AI Act draft (Obernolte–Trahan) is the first serious bipartisan attempt at binding federal rules — and it deserves to pass only if it is fixed.

**What the draft gets right:**

- **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI and authorizes $100M/year (vs. ~$15M today).
- **Sec. 111** — published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, critical safety incident reporting, penalties up to $1M/day.
- **Sec. 112** — licensed independent auditors (Independent Verification Organizations).
- **Sec. 113** — whistleblower anti-retaliation protections.

**What FRC asks Energy & Commerce to change — five fixes:**

1. **Strike the Sec. 121 state-law freeze.** The draft would preempt state laws regulating AI model development for three years — freezing the only binding frontier safety laws in force (California SB 53, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, phasing in through Jan. 1, 2027; Illinois' new law). A federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling.
2. **Require 72-hour incident reporting.** Fifteen days is too slow when weights are stolen or control is lost (Sec. 111). Match New York's 72-hour standard, keep the 24-hour imminent-risk channel, and give every state attorney general automatic access — not opt-in.
3. **Verify before deploy.** Move Sec. 112 audits upstream: independent verification *before* a new frontier model is released, and give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority (Sec. 102) — its guidelines are currently voluntary.
4. **License frontier training runs.** Add a federal license for training runs above the Sec. 101 compute threshold — no license, no training run. The administration is already improvising de facto licensing with export controls; Congress should put it in statute, with due process.
5. **Match SB 53 on whistleblowers; fund CAISI for the job.** Sec. 113 should include anonymous channels and attorney's fees, as California law already requires, and CAISI should be authorized well above $100M/year (FRC recommends at least $250M).

**The politics:** In FRC's August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (MOE ±2.5): **74%** say Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; **63%** say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; **52%** are worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. The Senate rejected a 10-year state-law freeze 99–1 in July 2025.

**Bottom line:** Fix the draft and FRC will support it. The test is simple: binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

**Frontier Restraint Coalition** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers.
Contact: Daniel Osei, Policy Director — policy@frontierrestraint.org
"}

## The stakes are catastrophic. The federal standard must be binding.

The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, 2023 — 350+ signers, including lab leaders). Capabilities have outrun oversight: after this spring's Mythos cyber scare, the administration improvised export controls on a frontier model in June. Voluntary commitments have not held. The Great American AI Act draft (Obernolte–Trahan) is the first serious bipartisan attempt at binding federal rules — and deserves to pass once fixed.

**What the draft gets right:**

- **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI; authorizes $100M/year (vs. ~$15M today).
- **Sec. 111** — published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting, penalties up to $1M/day.
- **Sec. 112** — licensed independent auditors.
- **Sec. 113** — whistleblower anti-retaliation protections.

**Five fixes FRC asks Energy & Commerce to make:**

1. **Strike the Sec. 121 state-law freeze.** The draft preempts state laws on AI model development for three years — freezing the only binding frontier safety laws in force (California SB 53, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, phasing in through Jan. 1, 2027). A federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling.
2. **Require 72-hour incident reporting.** Fifteen days is too slow when weights are stolen or control is lost. Match New York's 72-hour standard, keep the 24-hour imminent-risk channel, and give every state attorney general automatic access — not opt-in.
3. **Verify before deploy.** Move Sec. 112 audits upstream: independent verification *before* a frontier model is released, and give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority — its guidelines are currently voluntary.
4. **License frontier training runs.** Add a federal license for training runs above the Sec. 101 compute threshold: no license, no training run. The administration is already improvising de facto licensing via export controls; put it in statute.
5. **Match SB 53 on whistleblowers; fund CAISI for the job.** Sec. 113 should add anonymous channels and attorney's fees, as California law already requires, and CAISI should be funded well above $100M/year (FRC: at least $250M).

**The politics:** FRC's Aug. 2026 national survey (1,512 registered voters, MOE ±2.5): **74%** want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; **63%** say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; **52%** worry advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. The Senate rejected a 10-year state-law freeze 99–1 in July 2025.

**Bottom line:** Fix the draft and FRC will support it. The test is simple: binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

**Frontier Restraint Coalition** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, independent researchers.
Contact: Daniel Osei, Policy Director — policy@frontierrestraint.org

Section numbers verified against the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the discussion draft text released June 4, 2026 (obernolte.house.gov; trahan.house.gov), cross-checked with Roll Call (June 4, 2026) and Future of Privacy Forum analysis (June 9, 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121 — Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development** (3-year preemption of state laws on AI model development) | **Oppose** | Strike entirely; replace with a savings clause making the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling, that states may exceed | It would freeze the only binding frontier-safety laws in force (CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL SB 315) during the fastest capability ramp in history. |
| **Sec. 111(f)–(g) — Critical safety incident reporting** (15 days; 24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious injury) | **Support with amendment** | Require reporting within 72 hours of discovery (match NY RAISE); keep the 24-hour imminent-risk channel; make reports go automatically to every state attorney general, not opt-in under Sec. 111(h) | Two weeks of silence after a weight theft or loss-of-control event is two weeks of preventable exposure. |
| **Sec. 101(7) — Definition of "critical safety incident"** | **Support with amendment** | Add incidents where a model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as SB 53 and RAISE already cover | A model that hides from its own oversight is exactly the failure this law exists to catch. |
| **Sec. 111 — Published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, penalties up to $1M/day** | **Support** | Keep as drafted; preserve the $1M/day penalty and federal injunction authority | Published safety plans backed by real penalties are the backbone of a binding regime. |
| **Sec. 112 — Independent Verification Organization (IVO) audits** (semi-annual, CAISI-licensed) | **Support with amendment** | Require IVO verification *before* deployment of any new frontier model or material modification, not only semi-annual look-backs; publish redacted audit summaries | Semi-annual after-the-fact audits inspect a horse that has already left the barn. |
| **Sec. 102 — CAISI codification; $100M/yr authorized FY2027–2029 (vs. ~$15M today); voluntary guidelines** | **Support with amendment** | Add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models; authorize funding well above $100M/yr (FRC recommends at least $250M); keep the above-GS hiring flexibility | A regulator that can only issue voluntary guidelines cannot verify the most dangerous systems ever built. |
| **No licensing provision** (absent from the draft) | **Ask to add** | Create a federal license for training runs above the Sec. 101 compute threshold — no license, no training run — renewable and conditioned on a published framework, IVO verification and model-weight security | The administration is already improvising de facto licensing through export controls; Congress should put it in statute with due process. |
| **Sec. 113 — Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections** (employees and contractors) | **Support with amendment** | Match SB 53: require anonymous internal disclosure channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, meaningful penalties, and an explicit statement that stronger state protections survive | The people inside these labs are the country's early-warning system. |
| **Sec. 101 — Frontier model threshold** (foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations) | **Support with amendment** | Require a periodic Commerce/CAISI review to update the threshold as training costs fall, and allow designation of a sub-threshold model as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk | The frontier of 2028 will not be the frontier of 2026, and coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker. |
| **Sec. 311 / Sec. 321 — CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; GAO report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security** | **Support** | Fund at requested levels and require the committee to act on the GAO report's findings | Stolen model weights are a catastrophic-risk pathway, and the people guarding them are underfunded. |
| **Sec. 132 — AI impersonation of federal officials** | **Support** | Keep as drafted | Trust in government communications is itself a safety asset. |

## Messaging anchors (per board-approved guide v3)

- The core ask in every meeting: **binding, not voluntary** — verify before deploy.
- On preemption: **a floor, not a ceiling** — no freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Name the stakes plainly: **catastrophic risk**, up to and including the extinction-level risk that the labs' own leaders have acknowledged (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023).
- Acknowledge AI's benefits in one sentence, then return to the frontier.
"}

**DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off. Answers ≤120 words each. For Hill meetings; pair with the one-pager and asks-by-section table.**

---

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Because both act after the fact, and CAISI's guidelines are voluntary. Reporting tells you what has already gone wrong; the draft's audits happen twice a year, after models are live. Nothing in the draft stops a developer from releasing a frontier model that fails every safety test — and Section 121 would strip the binding rules already in force in California and New York. That's why FRC asks for pre-deployment verification by licensed independent auditors, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, and a license to train at the frontier. Put simply: the draft tells us when a fire starts. We want the building inspected before it opens. Binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Shortened, no. A two-year or one-year freeze is still a freeze, imposed during the fastest capability ramp in history, on the only binding frontier safety laws in force — California's SB 53 now, New York's RAISE from January. The length of the window doesn't change the principle: a federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling. Dropped, yes. Strike Section 121 and strengthen the rest — 72-hour incident reporting, pre-deployment verification, mandatory CAISI testing, whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53, licensing for frontier training runs — and FRC would support the bill and advocate for it. We want to say yes to a bill like this. As drafted, we cannot.

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

Safety is how you stay ahead. A model whose weights are stolen, or that fails catastrophically, doesn't win anything for America — it hands the frontier to Beijing. Our advantage is trust: allies and buyers choose systems they can verify, and verification requires binding standards. The administration has conceded the point in practice: in June it used export controls to block foreign access to a frontier model it judged too dangerous to share, and it is weighing mandatory pre-deployment licensing. Nobody serious argues we should ship untested systems because China might. And voters aren't asking for that: 74% in our August survey want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Verify before deploy is a competitiveness strategy.

## 4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

Codifying CAISI is overdue, and $100 million a year is roughly seven times its current $15 million — real progress, and we support it. But the job is bigger than the number: licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, and monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly. FRC asks for four things: mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, since its guidelines are currently voluntary; authorization well above $100 million — at least $250 million a year; retention of the above-GS hiring flexibility in the draft, so it can compete for technical staff; and annual reporting to Congress so the authorization stays honest. A regulator that can only ask politely cannot verify the most dangerous systems ever built.
"}
