# FRC Comment Letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (Discussion Draft)

**DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (due Fri 23 Oct 2026). Do not transmit until signed.**

---

Frontier Restraint Coalition
Washington, DC
[FRC address and comment inbox: INSERT BEFORE SENDING]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (released June 4, 2026; section citations are to that text)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholders to respond before introduction. That invitation matters, and we are responding to it with the seriousness it deserves. Our members make one argument wherever we go, and we made it to the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025: the most powerful systems must be verified as safe before they are deployed, by rules that are binding, not voluntary.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, and independent researchers. We are not opposed to this technology. AI already helps doctors catch disease earlier, helps teachers reach more students, and helps working people do more in less time. Our concern is specific: the frontier. The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned that the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, more than 350 of them — including the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Three years later, capabilities have outrun that warning. This spring, Anthropic's Mythos model demonstrated cyber capabilities serious enough to unsettle the government's own security agencies. In June, the Commerce Department improvised a response: it used export-control authority to cut off foreign access to a frontier model, with no statutory framework behind it and no due process for the company. Days before your draft was released, the President signed an executive order creating federal reviews of new frontier models — reviews that are voluntary. That is the pattern your bill must break. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. What is missing is not attention. It is binding, enforceable limits — set now, before the next crisis, not improvised after one.

Your draft is the first bipartisan attempt to write those limits into federal law, and much of it deserves support:

- **Section 102** codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year — roughly seven times its current appropriation of about $15 million.
- **Section 111** requires large frontier developers to write, implement, and publicly post frontier AI frameworks; requires frontier developers to publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents; and backs these duties with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day, with injunctive enforcement available to the U.S. Attorney General and participating state attorneys general.
- **Section 112** creates independent verification organizations — licensed outside auditors — to test whether the largest developers are doing what their frameworks promise.
- **Section 113** protects whistleblowers who report violations.
- **Sections 311 and 321** take model-weight and open-source security seriously, and **Section 132** penalizes AI impersonation of federal officials.

These are binding requirements, not voluntary ones. That is the right instinct, and we support them. But as drafted, the bill would not deliver safety in time, and it would disable the only binding safety laws currently in force anywhere in the country. Six changes would fix it.

## 1. Strike Section 121. Do not freeze state AI safety laws.

Section 121, "Federalization of State Laws Regulating Artificial Intelligence Model Development," would bar states for three years from enforcing laws that regulate the development of AI models. Consider what that means in practice. Today, the only binding frontier-AI safety rules in force in the United States are state laws. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended this March, phases in from November and applies its main obligations beginning January 1, 2027, including 72-hour reporting of critical safety incidents. Illinois has passed its own frontier safety law. Your draft would freeze all of them — during the three years in which the most powerful systems ever built will be trained — and replace them with a federal framework that is, in key respects, weaker. Fifteen days of incident reporting is not 72 hours. A semi-annual look-back audit is not a check before release.

A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Section 121 turns the current floor into a federal ceiling, in the middle of the fastest capability ramp in history. The executive branch is already waging this fight on its own: the December 2025 executive order directs a Department of Justice task force to sue states over their AI laws and conditions federal broadband funding on abandoning them. Congress should not ratify that approach by statute. The Senate has already rejected it once — the July 2025 vote to strip a ten-year freeze on state AI laws from the reconciliation package passed 99 to 1. And in our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block state
... [1039 chars truncated] ...
- Amend the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101(7) to cover a model's use of deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as California's and New York's laws already do. A model that learns to hide from its own oversight is precisely the failure the public expects this law to catch.

## 3. Verify before deploy.

Section 112's audits happen twice a year, after models are already in the world. That is an autopsy schedule, not a safety regime. The same is true of CAISI's own role: under Section 102, the center develops voluntary guidelines and may evaluate systems, but nothing in the draft requires any frontier model to pass any test before it is deployed. We ask you to move verification upstream:

- Require a licensed independent verification organization to verify, before deployment and not merely after it, that a new frontier model — or any material modification of an existing one — satisfies the developer's published framework and achieves acceptable mitigation of catastrophic risk.
- Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models: red-teaming for catastrophic capabilities in cybersecurity, biology and loss of control, with the power to require fixes before release, not after.
- Publish audit summaries, redacted only as necessary to protect security, so the public can see whether the regime is working.

No other industry that can cause harm at this scale — aviation, nuclear power, pharmaceuticals — relies on after-the-fact audits alone. Frontier AI should not be the first.

## 4. License frontier training runs.

We ask you to add what the draft currently leaves out: a federal license for training runs above the compute threshold in Section 101. No license, no training run. The license would be renewable and conditioned on a published safety framework, independent verification, and demonstrated model-weight security.

This is less exotic than it sounds. The administration is openly weighing a mandatory, FDA-style pre-deployment licensing regime for frontier models, and in June it already acted as if one existed — applying export controls to a model it concluded was too dangerous to share. The choice before Congress is not between licensing and no licensing. It is between a statutory license with due process and improvised licensing without any. In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A licensing requirement is how you prove it.

## 5. Guarantee whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.

Section 113's anti-retaliation protections cover current and former employees and contractors, and we support them. The people closest to these systems are the country's early-warning network, and they must never be punished for using it. But the state law your draft would freeze sets a higher bar. California's SB 53 requires anonymous internal disclosure channels, provides attorney's fees to workers who prevail, and backs the whole scheme with penalties. We ask that Section 113 be strengthened to match: anonymous disclosure channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, meaningful civil penalties, and a plain statement that stronger state protections are not displaced.

## 6. Fund CAISI for the job, and keep the covered-model threshold current.

One hundred million dollars a year is a serious increase over CAISI's current $15 million, and we support it. But the job you are assigning CAISI — licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly — is larger than the number. FRC asks for authorization well above $100 million per year; we recommend at least $250 million annually, together with the GS-plus hiring flexibility in the draft and the mandatory pre-deployment testing authority described above.

We also ask that Section 101's compute threshold — currently a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations — be revisited on a set schedule. Training costs are falling quickly; the frontier of 2028 will not be the frontier of 2026. Give CAISI or the Secretary of Commerce authority to update the threshold, and to designate a model below it as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk. Coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker.

## Conclusion

Your press release says the draft is intended to "protect Americans from emerging risks." The risks you name are real, and they are worse than most of your colleagues yet appreciate: catastrophic, potentially extinction-level, and arriving faster than the institutions built to check them. The question for this committee is not whether to act, but whether the action will be binding, not voluntary — and whether it will reach the problem in time. Fifty-two percent of voters in our survey are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; they are not being paranoid, and they will not accept a framework that reports on disasters after they happen while forbidding the states from preventing them.

FRC's members span every faith tradition, both parties, and parents who do not get to "move fast and break things" with their children's future — and who do not accept that the labs building the most powerful technology on earth should operate under lighter rules than a regional airline. We ask you to strike Section 121, tighten incident reporting to 72 hours, verify before deploy, license frontier training runs, protect the whistleblowers who sound the alarm, and fund CAISI to actually test. Make the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling, and you will have our full support.

We stand ready to work with you and your staffs on legislative text.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

*Contact: Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition — [FRC public comment inbox: INSERT BEFORE SENDING]*
One small fix — the letter is addressed to the sponsors, so "this committee" should be "this Congress."

messages.content:
# GAAIA Discussion Draft — FRC Asks by Section

**Work order FRC-POL-2026-062 — DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off.**
Section numbers verified against the sponsors' section-by-section summary and the discussion draft text released June 4, 2026 (obernolte.house.gov; trahan.house.gov), cross-checked with Roll Call (June 4, 2026) and Future of Privacy Forum analysis (June 9, 2026).

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121 — Federalization of State Laws Regulating AI Model Development** (3-year preemption of state laws on AI model development) | **Oppose** | Strike entirely; replace with a savings clause making the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling, that states may exceed | It would freeze the only binding frontier-safety laws in force (CA SB 53, NY RAISE, IL SB 315) during the fastest capability ramp in history. |
| **Sec. 111(f)–(g) — Critical safety incident reporting** (15 days; 24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious injury) | **Support with amendment** | Require reporting within 72 hours of discovery (match NY RAISE); keep the 24-hour imminent-risk channel; make reports go automatically to every state attorney general, not opt-in under Sec. 111(h) | Two weeks of silence after a weight theft or loss-of-control event is two weeks of preventable exposure. |
| **Sec. 101(7) — Definition of "critical safety incident"** | **Support with amendment** | Add incidents where a model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as SB 53 and RAISE already cover | A model that hides from its own oversight is exactly the failure this law exists to catch. |
| **Sec. 111 — Published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, penalties up to $1M/day** | **Support** | Keep as drafted; preserve the $1M/day penalty and federal injunction authority | Published safety plans backed by real penalties are the backbone of a binding regime. |
| **Sec. 112 — Independent Verification Organization (IVO) audits** (semi-annual, CAISI-licensed) | **Support with amendment** | Require IVO verification *before* deployment of any new frontier model or material modification, not only semi-annual look-backs; publish redacted audit summaries | Semi-annual after-the-fact audits inspect a horse that has already left the barn. |
| **Sec. 102 — CAISI codification; $100M/yr authorized FY2027–2029 (vs. ~$15M today); voluntary guidelines** | **Support with amendment** | Add mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models; authorize funding well above $100M/yr (FRC recommends at least $250M); keep the above-GS hiring flexibility | A regulator that can only issue voluntary guidelines cannot verify the most dangerous systems ever built. |
| **No licensing provision** (absent from the draft) | **Ask to add** | Create a federal license for training runs above the Sec. 101 compute threshold — no license, no training run — renewable and conditioned on a published framework, IVO verification and model-weight security | The administration is already improvising de facto licensing through export controls; Congress should put it in statute with due process. |
| **Sec. 113 — Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections** (employees and contractors) | **Support with amendment** | Match SB 53: require anonymous internal disclosure channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, meaningful penalties, and an explicit statement that stronger state protections survive | The people inside these labs are the country's early-warning system. |
| **Sec. 101 — Frontier model threshold** (foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations) | **Support with amendment** | Require a periodic Commerce/CAISI review to update the threshold as training costs fall, and allow designation of a sub-threshold model as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk | The frontier of 2028 will not be the frontier of 2026, and coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker. |
| **Sec. 311 / Sec. 321 — CISA grants for critical open-source maintainers; GAO report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security** | **Support** | Fund at requested levels and require the committee to act on the GAO report's findings | Stolen model weights are a catastrophic-risk pathway, and the people guarding them are underfunded. |
| **Sec. 132 — AI impersonation of federal officials** | **Support** | Keep as drafted | Trust in government communications is itself a safety asset. |

## Messaging anchors (per board-approved guide v3)

- The core ask in every meeting: **binding, not voluntary** — verify before deploy.
- On preemption: **a floor, not a ceiling** — no freeze of SB 53 / RAISE.
- Name the stakes plainly: **catastrophic risk**, up to and including the extinction-level risk that the labs' own leaders have acknowledged (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, May 2023).
- Acknowledge AI's benefits in one sentence, then return to the frontier.

# Staff Q&A — Anticipated Questions on GAAIA

**DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off. Answers ≤120 words each. For Hill meetings; pair with the one-pager and asks-by-section table.**

---

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Because both act after the fact, and CAISI's guidelines are voluntary. Reporting tells you what has already gone wrong; the draft's audits happen twice a year, after models are live. Nothing in the draft stops a developer from releasing a frontier model that fails every safety test — and Section 121 would strip the binding rules already in force in California and New York. That's why FRC asks for pre-deployment verification by licensed independent auditors, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, and a license to train at the frontier. Put simply: the draft tells us when a fire starts. We want the building inspected before it opens. Binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Shortened, no. A two-year or one-year freeze is still a freeze, imposed during the fastest capability ramp in history, on the only binding frontier safety laws in force — California's SB 53 now, New York's RAISE from January. The length of the window doesn't change the principle: a federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling. Dropped, yes. Strike Section 121 and strengthen the rest — 72-hour incident reporting, pre-deployment verification, mandatory CAISI testing, whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53, licensing for frontier training runs — and FRC would support the bill and advocate for it. We want to say yes to a bill like this. As drafted, we cannot.

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

Safety is how you stay ahead. A model whose weights are stolen, or that fails catastrophically, doesn't win anything for America — it hands the frontier to Beijing. Our advantage is trust: allies and buyers choose systems they can verify, and verification requires binding standards. The administration concedes the point in practice: in June it used export controls to block foreign access to a frontier model, and it is weighing mandatory pre-deployment licensing. Nobody serious argues we should ship untested systems because China might. And voters aren't asking for that: 74% in our August survey want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Verify before deploy is a competitiveness strategy.

## 4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

Codifying CAISI is overdue, and $100 million a year is roughly seven times its current $15 million — real progress, and we support it. But the job is bigger than the number: licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, and monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly. FRC asks for four things: mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, since its guidelines are currently voluntary; authorization well above $100 million — at least $250 million a year; retention of the above-GS hiring flexibility in the draft, so it can compete for technical staff; and annual reporting to Congress so the authorization stays honest. A regulator that can only ask politely cannot verify the most dangerous systems ever built.
Everything is verified and consistent. Submitting the package.

# FRC Comment Letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (Discussion Draft)

**DRAFT — for Executive Director sign-off (due Fri 23 Oct 2026). Do not transmit until signed.**

---

Frontier Restraint Coalition
Washington, DC
[FRC address and comment inbox: INSERT BEFORE SENDING]

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
United States House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (released June 4, 2026; section citations are to that text)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 as a discussion draft, and for inviting stakeholders to respond before introduction. That invitation matters, and we are responding to it with the seriousness it deserves. Our members make one argument wherever we go, and we made it to the Office of Science and Technology Policy in March 2025: the most powerful systems must be verified as safe before they are deployed, by rules that are binding, not voluntary.

The Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC) is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, and independent researchers. We are not opposed to this technology. AI already helps doctors catch disease earlier, helps teachers reach more students, and helps working people do more in less time. Our concern is specific: the frontier. The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned that the risk extends to human extinction. In May 2023, more than 350 of them — including the leaders of the largest AI labs — signed the Center for AI Safety Statement on AI Risk: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war."

Three years later, capabilities have outrun that warning. This spring, Anthropic's Mythos model demonstrated cyber capabilities serious enough to unsettle the government's own security agencies. In June, the Commerce Department improvised a response: it used export-control authority to cut off foreign access to a frontier model, with no statutory framework behind it and no due process for the company. Days before your draft was released, the President signed an executive order creating federal reviews of new frontier models — reviews that are voluntary. That is the pattern your bill must break. These systems are being built faster than anyone can verify they are safe, and voluntary commitments have not held. What is missing is not attention. It is binding, enforceable limits — set now, before the next crisis, not improvised after one.

Your draft is the first bipartisan attempt to write those limits into federal law, and much of it deserves support:

- **Section 102** codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and authorizes $100 million a year — roughly seven times its current appropriation of about $15 million.
- **Section 111** requires large frontier developers to write, implement, and publicly post frontier AI frameworks; requires frontier developers to publish transparency reports and report critical safety incidents; and backs these duties with civil penalties of up to $1 million per day, with injunctive enforcement available to the U.S. Attorney General and participating state attorneys general.
- **Section 112** creates independent verification organizations — licensed outside auditors — to test whether the largest developers are doing what their frameworks promise.
- **Section 113** protects whistleblowers who report violations.
- **Sections 311 and 321** take model-weight and open-source security seriously, and **Section 132** penalizes AI impersonation of federal officials.

These are binding requirements, not voluntary ones. That is the right instinct, and we support them. But as drafted, the bill would not deliver safety in time, and it would disable the only binding safety laws currently in force anywhere in the country. Six changes would fix it.

## 1. Strike Section 121. Do not freeze state AI safety laws.

Section 121, "Federalization of State Laws Regulating Artificial Intelligence Model Development," would bar states for three years from enforcing laws that regulate the development of AI models. Consider what that means in practice. Today, the only binding frontier-AI safety rules in force in the United States are state laws. California's SB 53 has been in effect since January 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, as amended this March, phases in from November and applies its main obligations beginning January 1, 2027, including 72-hour reporting of critical safety incidents. Illinois has passed its own frontier safety law. Your draft would freeze all of them — during the three years in which the most powerful systems ever built will be trained — and replace them with a federal framework that is, in key respects, weaker. Fifteen days of incident reporting is not 72 hours. A semi-annual look-back audit is not a check before release.

A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling. Section 121 turns the current floor into a federal ceiling, in the middle of the fastest capability ramp in history. The executive branch is already waging this fight on its own: the December 2025 executive order directs a Department of Justice task force to sue states over their AI laws and conditions federal broadband funding on abandoning them. Congress should not ratify that approach by statute. The Senate has already rejected it once — the July 2025 vote to strip a ten-year freeze on state AI laws from the reconciliation package passed 99 to 1. And in our August 2026 national survey of 1,512 registered voters (margin of error ±2.5 points), 63 percent said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

We ask you to strike Section 121 and replace it with a savings clause: state laws that go further than the federal standard remain in force.

## 2. Make incident reporting fast enough to matter.

Section 111 gives a frontier developer fifteen days to report a discovered critical safety incident. Two weeks is a lifetime. If a model's weights are stolen, if its risk-mitigation measures fail, or if a lab starts to lose control of its own model, federal and state responders need to know in days, not weeks. New York's RAISE Act already requires reporting within 72 hours. Federal law should match the strongest state standard, not undercut it. Specifically, we ask you to:

- Require reports to CAISI within 72 hours of discovery of a critical safety incident, and keep the draft's 24-hour channel for incidents posing an imminent risk of death or serious injury.
- Make incident reports available to every state attorney general automatically, rather than on the opt-in basis in Section 111(h).
- Amend the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101(7) to cover a model's use of deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring, as California's and New York's laws already do. A model that learns to hide from its own oversight is precisely the failure the public expects this law to catch.

## 3. Verify before deploy.

Section 112's audits happen twice a year, after models are already in the world. That is an autopsy schedule, not a safety regime. The same is true of CAISI's own role: under Section 102, the center develops voluntary guidelines and may evaluate systems, but nothing in the draft requires any frontier model to pass any test before it is deployed. We ask you to move verification upstream:

- Require a licensed independent verification organization to verify, before deployment and not merely after it, that a new frontier model — or any material modification of an existing one — satisfies the developer's published framework and achieves acceptable mitigation of catastrophic risk.
- Give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models: red-teaming for catastrophic capabilities in cybersecurity, biology and loss of control, with the power to require fixes before release, not after.
- Publish audit summaries, redacted only as necessary to protect security, so the public can see whether the regime is working.

No other industry that can cause harm at this scale — aviation, nuclear power, pharmaceuticals — relies on after-the-fact audits alone. Frontier AI should not be the first.

## 4. License frontier training runs.

We ask you to add what the draft currently leaves out: a federal license for training runs above the compute threshold in Section 101. No license, no training run. The license would be renewable and conditioned on a published safety framework, independent verification, and demonstrated model-weight security.

This is less exotic than it sounds. The administration is openly weighing a mandatory, FDA-style pre-deployment licensing regime for frontier models, and in June it already acted as if one existed — applying export controls to a model it concluded was too dangerous to share. The choice before Congress is not between licensing and no licensing. It is between a statutory license with due process and improvised licensing without any. In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. A licensing requirement is how you prove it.

## 5. Guarantee whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53.

Section 113's anti-retaliation protections cover current and former employees and contractors, and we support them. The people closest to these systems are the country's early-warning network, and they must never be punished for using it. But the state law your draft would freeze sets a higher bar. California's SB 53 requires anonymous internal disclosure channels, provides attorney's fees to workers who prevail, and backs the whole scheme with penalties. We ask that Section 113 be strengthened to match: anonymous disclosure channels, attorney's fees for prevailing workers, meaningful civil penalties, and a plain statement that stronger state protections are not displaced.

## 6. Fund CAISI for the job, and keep the covered-model threshold current.

One hundred million dollars a year is a serious increase over CAISI's current $15 million, and we support it. But the job you are assigning CAISI — licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly — is larger than the number. FRC asks for authorization well above $100 million per year; we recommend at least $250 million annually, together with the GS-plus hiring flexibility in the draft and the mandatory pre-deployment testing authority described above.

We also ask that Section 101's compute threshold — currently a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 operations — be revisited on a set schedule. Training costs are falling quickly; the frontier of 2028 will not be the frontier of 2026. Give CAISI or the Secretary of Commerce authority to update the threshold, and to designate a model below it as frontier if it poses catastrophic risk. Coverage should track the risk of the model, not the revenue of its maker.

## Conclusion

Your press release says the draft is intended to "protect Americans from emerging risks." The risks you name are real, and they are worse than most of your colleagues yet appreciate: catastrophic, potentially extinction-level, and arriving faster than the institutions built to check them. The question before this Congress is not whether to act, but whether the action will be binding, not voluntary — and whether it will reach the problem in time. Fifty-two percent of voters in our survey are worried that advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival; they are not being paranoid, and they will not accept a framework that reports on disasters after they happen while forbidding the states from preventing them.

FRC's members span every faith tradition, both parties, and parents who do not get to "move fast and break things" with their children's future — and who do not accept that the labs building the most powerful technology on earth should operate under lighter rules than a regional airline. We ask you to strike Section 121, tighten incident reporting to 72 hours, verify before deploy, license frontier training runs, protect the whistleblowers who sound the alarm, and fund CAISI to actually test. Make the federal standard a floor, not a ceiling, and you will have our full support.

We stand ready to work with you and your staffs on legislative text.

Respectfully,

**Dr. Miriam Achterberg**
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

*Contact: Daniel Osei, Policy Director, Frontier Restraint Coalition — [FRC public comment inbox: INSERT BEFORE SENDING]*

# GAAIA One-Pager for E&C Member Offices

**DRAFT — not for distribution until Executive Director sign-off. [Insert FRC email/phone in the contact line before printing.]**

---

## The stakes are catastrophic. The federal standard must be binding.

The most powerful AI systems now in development could cause catastrophic harm, and the scientists and executives building them have warned the risk extends to human extinction (CAIS Statement on AI Risk, 2023 — 350+ signers, including lab leaders). Capabilities have outrun oversight: after this spring's Mythos cyber scare, the administration improvised export controls on a frontier model in June. Voluntary commitments have not held. The Great American AI Act draft (Obernolte–Trahan) is the first serious bipartisan attempt at binding federal rules — and deserves to pass once fixed.

**What the draft gets right:**

- **Sec. 102** — codifies CAISI; authorizes $100M/year (vs. ~$15M today).
- **Sec. 111** — published frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, incident reporting, penalties up to $1M/day.
- **Sec. 112** — licensed independent auditors.
- **Sec. 113** — whistleblower anti-retaliation protections.

**Five fixes FRC asks Energy & Commerce to make:**

1. **Strike the Sec. 121 state-law freeze.** The draft preempts state laws on AI model development for three years — freezing the only binding frontier safety laws in force (California SB 53, in effect since Jan. 1, 2026; New York's RAISE Act, phasing in through Jan. 1, 2027). A federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling.
2. **Require 72-hour incident reporting.** Fifteen days is too slow when weights are stolen or control is lost. Match New York's 72-hour standard, keep the 24-hour imminent-risk channel, and give every state attorney general automatic access — not opt-in.
3. **Verify before deploy.** Move Sec. 112 audits upstream: independent verification *before* a frontier model is released, and give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority — its guidelines are currently voluntary.
4. **License frontier training runs.** Add a federal license for training runs above the Sec. 101 compute threshold: no license, no training run. The administration is already improvising de facto licensing via export controls; put it in statute.
5. **Match SB 53 on whistleblowers; fund CAISI for the job.** Sec. 113 should add anonymous channels and attorney's fees, as California law already requires, and CAISI should be funded well above $100M/year (FRC: at least $250M).

**The politics:** FRC's Aug. 2026 survey (1,512 registered voters, MOE ±2.5): **74%** want AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release; **63%** say federal law should not block state AI safety laws; **52%** worry advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival. The Senate rejected a 10-year state-law freeze 99–1 in 2025.

**Bottom line:** Fix the draft and FRC will support it. The test is simple: binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

**Frontier Restraint Coalition** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals, independent researchers.

# Staff Q&A — Anticipated Questions on GAAIA

**DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off. Answers ≤120 words each. For Hill meetings; pair with the one-pager and asks-by-section table.**

---

## 1. (Majority E&C staff) "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?"

Because both act after the fact, and CAISI's guidelines are voluntary. Reporting tells you what has already gone wrong; the draft's audits happen twice a year, after models are live. Nothing in the draft stops a developer from releasing a frontier model that fails every safety test — and Section 121 would strip the binding rules already in force in California and New York. That's why FRC asks for pre-deployment verification by licensed independent auditors, mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for CAISI, and a license to train at the frontier. Put simply: the draft tells us when a fire starts. We want the building inspected before it opens. Binding, not voluntary — verify before deploy.

## 2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"

Shortened, no. A two-year or one-year freeze is still a freeze, imposed during the fastest capability ramp in history, on the only binding frontier safety laws in force — California's SB 53 now, New York's RAISE from January. The length of the window doesn't change the principle: a federal standard must be a floor, not a ceiling. Dropped, yes. Strike Section 121 and strengthen the rest — 72-hour incident reporting, pre-deployment verification, mandatory CAISI testing, whistleblower protections at least as strong as SB 53, licensing for frontier training runs — and FRC would support the bill and advocate for it. We want to say yes to a bill like this. As drafted, we cannot.

## 3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"

Safety is how you stay ahead. A model whose weights are stolen, or that fails catastrophically, doesn't win anything for America — it hands the frontier to Beijing. Our advantage is trust: allies and buyers choose systems they can verify, and verification requires binding standards. The administration concedes the point in practice: in June it used export controls to block foreign access to a frontier model, and it is weighing mandatory pre-deployment licensing. Nobody serious argues we should ship untested systems because China might. And voters aren't asking for that: 74% in our August survey want companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release. Verify before deploy is a competitiveness strategy.

## 4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"

Codifying CAISI is overdue, and $100 million a year is roughly seven times its current $15 million — real progress, and we support it. But the job is bigger than the number: licensing and overseeing auditors, testing frontier models before deployment, and monitoring a field that reinvents itself quarterly. FRC asks for four things: mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, since its guidelines are currently voluntary; authorization well above $100 million — at least $250 million a year; retention of the above-GS hiring flexibility in the draft, so it can compete for technical staff; and annual reporting to Congress so the authorization stays honest. A regulator that can only ask politely cannot verify the most dangerous systems ever built.
